title: Advance care planning when you live with arthritis and frailty (UK)
meta_title: Advance Care Planning With Arthritis and Frailty: A UK Guide

direct_answer: Advance care planning means thinking about and writing down what matters to you about future care, so your wishes are known if you become too unwell to say. It can include an advance statement, an advance decision to refuse treatment, a lasting power of attorney and conversations about resuscitation.

content:
Advance care planning is a way of thinking ahead about the care you would want if your health gets worse. It is not only about the end of life. It can cover where you would prefer to be cared for, what matters most to you day to day, and who should speak for you if you cannot.

If you live with arthritis and frailty, planning ahead can make hospital stays, falls and changes in health less stressful for you and your family. This guide explains the main options in the UK. It is educational information, not legal or medical advice.

What it can include

  • An advance statement: your wishes, values and preferences, such as where you would like to be cared for, how you like your pain managed, or your faith needs. It is not legally binding, but professionals should take it into account.
  • An advance decision to refuse treatment: a legally binding decision to refuse specific treatments in specific situations. To refuse life-sustaining treatment, it must be written, signed, witnessed and say clearly that it applies even if your life is at risk.
  • A lasting power of attorney (LPA): a legal document that lets someone you trust make decisions for you. There are separate LPAs for health and welfare, and for property and financial affairs.
  • Resuscitation decisions (DNACPR): a decision about whether CPR would be attempted, made with your clinicians. You can ask to discuss this.

Differences across the UK

The rules described above apply in England and Wales. Scotland uses a power of attorney under different law, and Northern Ireland has its own arrangements, which have been changing. Check with your GP, a solicitor or a local advice service about what applies where you live.

Why it matters with arthritis and frailty

Frailty can mean that an infection, fall or hospital stay has a bigger effect. Thinking ahead lets you say what matters to you, for example staying at home, avoiding certain treatments, or having pain well controlled, before a crisis.

Talking with family

  • Choose a calm time, not during an illness or a busy appointment.
  • Start with what matters to you, such as staying independent or being comfortable.
  • A family meeting with your GP, nurse or social worker present can help everyone hear the same information.
  • Write things down and share copies with the people who need them.

Getting started

  • Ask your GP or practice nurse about advance care planning. Some areas use a written plan that ambulance and hospital teams can see.
  • Think about who you would trust to speak for you.
  • Review your plan if your health or wishes change.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is it only for people near the end of life?

No. It can be done at any time and is often easier while you are well.

Can I change my mind?

Yes. You can change or cancel your plans while you have the capacity to decide.

Does a DNACPR mean no other treatment?

No. It only applies to CPR. Other treatment should continue as appropriate.
